headline: A 2014 Senate bill that was not adopted would have raised the federal minimum wage in stages to $10.10 an hour and changed tipped worker pay and some business tax rules.
what_it_does: If adopted, this bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps, starting at $8.20 an hour and reaching $10.10 an hour after two years, then adjusting by inflation each year. It would have raised the minimum cash wage for tipped workers to $3.00 an hour for one year, with later increases tied to 70% of the regular minimum wage. It would also have extended certain business expensing and depreciation tax treatment through taxable years before 2017.

who_it_affects.group: Workers paid the federal minimum wage
who_it_affects.how: Their hourly pay floor would have risen in steps to $10.10 an hour, then been adjusted for inflation.

who_it_affects.group: Tipped workers, such as restaurant servers
who_it_affects.how: Their required cash wage would have risen to $3.00 an hour for one year, then moved toward 70% of the regular minimum wage.

who_it_affects.group: Employers that pay the federal minimum wage or use tipped workers
who_it_affects.how: They would have had to pay higher hourly wages and higher cash wages for tipped employees on the bill's schedule.

who_it_affects.group: Businesses that buy equipment, software, or make leasehold or restaurant improvements
who_it_affects.how: They would have been able to keep the higher expensing allowance and depreciation treatment for taxable years before 2017.
It would have had to publish each wage increase in the Federal Register and on its website at least 60 days before it took effect.
